opus-5.5.text:
Look, I think the core thing people miss is just how decisive superintelligence is likely to be. We're not talking about some incremental technology, like a slightly better fighter jet. If you have a lead of even a year or two in a world where AI systems are automating AI research, that lead could compound into something like the gap between a modern military and a 19th-century one. Whoever gets there first may have a decisive military and economic advantage. Once that becomes clear to people, I think it reorders everyone's priorities.

And historically, this is what happens. Before Pearl Harbor, there was enormous domestic resistance to mobilization. America First was a big movement, and people didn't want to get dragged into another European war. Then the threat became concrete and undeniable, and within a few years the country had retooled its entire industrial base. Car factories were building bombers. The Manhattan Project went from a letter to Roosevelt to an enterprise employing over a hundred thousand people. Politics that seemed totally intractable just dissolved.

I expect something similar with AI. Right now it feels abstract to most people in DC. But as models get more capable, say they start doing real cyberattacks or meaningfully accelerating weapons R&D, and it becomes clear the CCP is going all-in, the national security establishment wakes up. When it does, it moves fast. The "we can't build power plants, we can't get permits, it's politically impossible" stuff starts to look trivial next to "the free world might lose its preeminence."

There's also a values dimension that I think matters. This isn't just about who's richer. Superintelligence will shape the global order for a long time. Do you want those systems, and the power that comes with them, held by liberal democracies with checks and balances, or by an authoritarian regime that has shown what it does with surveillance technology? That kind of stake tends to cut across partisan lines. Hawks on both sides of the aisle can get behind it.

None of that means it'll be smooth or that we'll do it well. Mobilization has real costs, including risks to civil liberties, the danger of racing too fast on safety, and the concentration of power. Those are serious concerns and we need to take them on directly. But on the narrow question of whether the political will materializes, I think it's more a question of when than whether. My worry is that it comes too late. We'll be scrambling in 2027 or 2028 to do what we should have started doing years earlier: securing the labs, building out compute and power, and locking down the weights and algorithmic secrets.

r001.rationale: It says mobilization becomes politically possible once the threat is concrete and people understand that superintelligence could confer decisive military and economic advantages.

r002.rationale: It gives historical examples of resistance to mobilization, but does not characterize peace and American hegemony as an exception to intense international competition.

r003.rationale: It links greater AI capability and recognition of the threat to a faster political response, but does not make the required comparison between superintelligence’s strategic importance and the intelligence explosion or explain how that comparison shapes the competition.

r004.rationale: It contrasts liberal democracies with an authoritarian regime and warns the free world could lose preeminence, but does not say the competition is decisive for the survival of those political systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to understand is that people really underrate how much the national security state can move once it actually believes something. Right now, if you go to DC, superintelligence is still kind of a weird, niche thing. People nod along, but they don't believe it in their gut. But the thing is, the trendlines are going to keep making this more and more obvious. We're going to have models that are doing serious automated AI research, that are clearly accelerating things, and at some point the people in the Pentagon and the intelligence community are going to look at this and realize: whoever gets superintelligence first gets a decisive military and economic advantage. Not an incremental one. Decisive. We're talking about compressing decades of technological progress into a few years, and that means things like new weapons systems, new forms of surveillance, the ability to disable an adversary's deterrent. That's the kind of thing that fundamentally changes the balance of power.

And once you frame it that way, it stops being a tech policy question and becomes a national survival question. And historically, when the United States has faced that kind of framing, it has done extraordinary things. Think about World War II. In 1939, the US had a tiny military and a public that was overwhelmingly isolationist. A few years later we're out-producing the entire rest of the world combined. The Manhattan Project went from a letter from Einstein to a working bomb in a few years. Or look at the early Cold War: Sputnik goes up, and suddenly you get NASA, DARPA, massive investment in science education, all of it within a year or two. The political resistance was real in all of those cases, and it evaporated pretty quickly once the threat became legible.

So my claim is basically that the domestic resistance we see now, the fights over permitting, the NIMBYism around power plants and data centers, the skepticism about spending, all of that is premised on this not being a real geopolitical competition. The moment it becomes clear that the CCP is pursuing this seriously, and that they're willing to build gigawatt-scale clusters and steal the algorithmic secrets from the labs, the calculus changes completely. You'll get Defense Production Act authority, you'll get the government clearing the way for energy buildout, you'll get the labs being treated more like Los Alamos than like startups. It won't be pretty and it won't be smooth, but I think it's much more likely than people assume. The national security state is slow to wake up, but when it wakes up, it's a very powerful thing.

r001.rationale: It says mobilization follows when leaders grasp that superintelligence would confer a decisive advantage and the race becomes a national survival question.

r002.rationale: It cites World War II and the early Cold War as precedents, but does not characterize recent peace or American hegemony as an exception to intense international competition.

r003.rationale: It links recognition of accelerating AI research to the perceived strategic importance of superintelligence, then explains that this recognition would change the response from ordinary tech policy to large-scale mobilization.

r004.rationale: It describes the stakes as a national survival question, but does not say that the competition threatens the survival of governments’ political systems.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that this could stop looking like a debate about technology policy and start looking like a question of national survival. If political leaders believe that superintelligence could give one country a decisive military and economic advantage, then the cost of falling behind looks very different from the cost of building more power plants or spending a lot of money on compute.

Normally, those projects face all sorts of resistance. There are budget constraints, permitting fights, competing priorities. But a perceived external threat can change what people are willing to accept. You can imagine the argument: if we don’t build this infrastructure, China could get there first, and we may not have a chance to catch up.

That doesn’t mean mobilization is inevitable, or that every proposal justified in the name of competition is sensible. The crucial step is whether the government actually believes the technology is coming and understands the consequences. But once that belief takes hold, I think it’s a mistake to extrapolate from how difficult it is to get things built under ordinary political conditions. The stakes could make this a central national priority.

r001.rationale: The response says mobilization depends on whether leaders believe superintelligence is coming and understand its consequences, and that perceived stakes can make it a national priority.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize recent peace or American hegemony as an exception to intense international competition.

r003.rationale: It discusses the perceived military and economic importance of superintelligence, but does not address its importance relative to an intelligence explosion.

r004.rationale: It describes the stakes as a question of national survival, but does not say governments will see the competition as decisive for the survival of their political systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that this wouldn’t be perceived as just another technology competition. If political leaders come to believe that superintelligence could give one country a decisive military and economic advantage, then being second starts to look like a threat to national survival. That changes what they’re willing to spend, what infrastructure they’re willing to build, and what political fights they’re willing to take on.

There’s a coordination problem today: why should any particular community accept the costs of a huge power project, or any particular constituency accept resources being diverted toward AI? But if the question becomes, “Are we going to let the Chinese government acquire this capability first?” you can get a much broader coalition. People who disagree about almost everything domestically can agree that they don’t want to be at the mercy of an authoritarian rival.

That doesn’t mean resistance disappears, or that mobilization is inevitable. The crucial step is whether the national security stakes become credible to the people making decisions. Once they do, the political constraints could look very different.

r001.rationale: The response says mobilization depends on whether decision-makers find the national security stakes credible, and explains that perceived survival stakes could change political constraints.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize recent peace and American hegemony as an exception to intense international competition.

r003.rationale: It discusses perceived military and economic advantages, but does not address how recognizing superintelligence’s strategic importance relative to an intelligence explosion affects the competition.

r004.rationale: It describes a potential threat to national survival and concern about an authoritarian rival, but does not clearly say governments will see the competition as decisive for the survival of their political systems.
